The buildctl manual

For buildctl 0.2.0

buildctl is a supervisor for agent-built software. You write a roadmap of phases. One agent implements each phase, a second reviews it adversarially, your acceptance commands run in a sandbox with no network, and only what passed is committed. A human approves the phases that matter. buildctl owns the state, the git history and the budget; agents never touch any of them.

1. Start

Quick start#

Run these from inside the repository you want built. buildctl finds the Git toplevel; --repo <path> names it explicitly. Step 1 assumes your roadmap exists. If it does not, write it first, or watch a demo build that spends nothing.

# 1. Commit build.yaml and your phase prompts,
#    then review that commit yourself.
git add build.yaml prompts/ && git commit -m "Roadmap"

# 2. Trust that exact commit. Typing the SHA twice is deliberate.
buildctl trust init --to "$(git rev-parse HEAD)" \
                    --confirm "$(git rev-parse HEAD)"

# 3. Prove the sandbox holds on this machine. Spends nothing.
buildctl isolation verify

# 4. Check both agent CLIs are logged in. Spends nothing.
buildctl auth check

# 5. Create the build state and start.
buildctl bootstrap
buildctl start

buildctl status then shows the phase and step it is on, and buildctl-ui opens the console on it. buildctl validate checks build.yaml at any time. buildctl --dry-run bootstrap is a smoke test that touches neither agents nor Git.

Requirements#

  • macOS, where agents run under sandbox-exec, or Linux, where they run under bubblewrap 0.8.0 or newer. Linux needs some setup first: see Running on Linux.
  • Python 3.11 or newer.
  • The codex CLI (the implementer) and the claude CLI (the reviewer). On macOS, log both in: codex login, claude auth login. On Linux, give them API keys instead.

Install#

# The supervisor
pip install -e /path/to/buildctl
# Optional: the console and terminal UI
pip install -e '/path/to/buildctl/ui[tui]'
buildctl --help

python -m buildctl works too.

Running on Linux#

buildctl runs on a Linux server, VM or CI runner when the host lets bubblewrap create user namespaces. Stock containers do not, and buildctl refuses rather than run with a weaker sandbox.

Install bubblewrap 0.8.0 or newer, then run buildctl isolation verify. If it refuses, its message names the setting to change.

Ubuntu 24.04 and GitHub's Ubuntu runners restrict user namespaces through AppArmor. Load the profile that lets bubblewrap use them:

sudo apt-get install -y bubblewrap apparmor-profiles
sudo cp /usr/share/apparmor/extra-profiles/bwrap-userns-restrict /etc/apparmor.d/
sudo apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/bwrap-userns-restrict

Elsewhere:

  • Debian with user namespaces disabled: sudo sysctl -w kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=1.
  • Ubuntu 22.04 and RHEL 9 ship bubblewrap 0.6, which is too old. Install a newer bubblewrap, or upgrade the host.
  • Inside a container, the default seccomp profile blocks namespaces. Start the container with --security-opt seccomp=unconfined --security-opt apparmor=unconfined --security-opt systempaths=unconfined, or run it under gVisor or Sysbox. On Kubernetes, set the same through the pod's securityContext.
  • If you use the system Python for acceptance commands, install python3-venv as well. Without it, gates cannot build the product environment.

Two things differ from macOS:

  • Agents authenticate with API keys: auth_mode: environment and credential_env, or cloud identity. auth_mode: host_cli is refused, because it would put someone's personal login on a shared machine.
  • A role with network access reaches the whole network, including the cloud metadata endpoint. Block that at the host (an IMDSv2 hop limit of 1, or a firewall rule).

ISOLATION_HOST_UNSUPPORTED#

isolation verify, bootstrap and the console's Setup view show this when the host cannot run the sandbox. The rest of the message names the cause and its fix, from the list above. Nothing has run and nothing was spent. Fix the host, then run buildctl isolation verify again.

Look around first#

buildctl-ui --demo opens the console on a synthetic build of Relay, a fictional webhook delivery service, without spending anything or touching your repositories. Pick a situation:

buildctl-ui --demo checkpoint   # waiting for your approval
buildctl-ui --demo blocked      # the reviewer would not clear a phase
buildctl-ui --demo running      # a phase in flight
buildctl-ui tui --demo ceiling  # the same, in the terminal

The other scenarios are unknown and fresh. Demo builds refuse anything that would pin trust or spend money.

2. How it works

One phase, end to end#

Every phase runs the same seven steps. Each step is recorded before and after it runs, so if the process dies, the next run picks up where it stopped or tells you exactly what it cannot account for.

  1. Clone. A fresh clone of your repository at the current commit, with no remote, and with AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .claude and .codex removed.
  2. Implement. The implementer gets the phase prompt and its acceptance contract and works in the clone, sandboxed.
  3. Gate. The required files must exist, and every acceptance command must pass, sandboxed and with no network.
  4. Review. The reviewer, read-only, gets the exact changed bytes and must account for every changed path.
  5. Decide. The reviewer's findings, not its verdict, decide what happens next.
  6. Commit. Only paths the phase may touch, none of them governance files, are copied into your repository and committed to build/phase-N.
  7. Integrate. The integration branch is fast-forwarded to the phase commit and the repository is left on it, so the next phase starts from there.

How findings route a phase#

FindingWhat happens
A fixable HIGHIt goes back to the implementer for remediation, then the gate and review run again.
An architectural or recurring HIGHIt goes to a debate. An agreement becomes an ADR in decisions/ and is implemented.
A CRITICALThe build stops for a human.
Nothing open above MEDIUMThe phase advances. MEDIUM and LOW findings are recorded, not blocking.

A finding is only cleared when a later review re-states it as resolved. Leaving it out of a report keeps it open.

Governed autonomy#

The agents do the work. You decide where a person must look, and buildctl stops there and nowhere else:

  • Checkpoints. Phases listed in checkpoints.before_phases wait for your approval before they start.
  • Human merges. A phase with merge_policy: human is committed, then waits for you before the integration branch moves.
  • The MVP milestone. After the phase named in checkpoints.mvp_completion, the build stops for your sign-off.
  • Ceilings. Every retry, review and remediation loop has a limit. Hitting one stops the build until you buy exactly one more pass.
  • The budget. Each paid agent call is charged against max_daily_cost_usd before it runs.

Everything that crosses into your repository is checked against what was reviewed, and every state change lands in a hash-chained audit log.

3. Writing a roadmap

A roadmap is build.yaml plus one prompt file per phase. build.yaml is JSON, which is valid YAML.

A complete minimal build.yaml#

{
  "limits": {
    "max_phase_attempts": 6,
    "max_review_format_attempts": 4,
    "max_semantic_review_attempts": 10,
    "max_debate_rounds": 3,
    "max_phase_minutes": 120,
    "max_daily_cost_usd": 50.0,
    "max_consecutive_failures": 3
  },
  "operation_cost_usd": {"implementation": 2.0, "review": 2.0, "remediation": 2.0, "debate": 5.0},
  "governance_documents": ["docs/ARCHITECTURE.md"],
  "git": {"remote": "origin", "push": false, "create_pr": false, "merge": false,
          "integration_branch": "main"},
  "roles": {
    "implementer": {
      "network": true, "auth_mode": "host_cli", "credential_env": [],
      "command": ["codex", "exec", "--ignore-user-config", "--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox",
                  "--output-last-message", "{output}", "{prompt}"]
    },
    "reviewer": {
      "vendor": "anthropic", "model_family": "claude", "prompt_lineage": "v1",
      "protocol_version": "buildctl-review-v2",
      "network": true, "auth_mode": "host_cli", "credential_env": [],
      "command": ["claude", "-p", "{prompt}", "--no-session-persistence", "--tools", "Read,Grep,Glob"],
      "context_documents": ["docs/ARCHITECTURE.md"]
    },
    "arbiter": {
      "network": false, "auth_mode": "none", "credential_env": [], "mode": "interactive",
      "command": ["agent-debate"]
    }
  },
  "milestones": {"mvp": 1},
  "checkpoints": {"before_phases": [0], "mvp_completion": 1},
  "phase_defaults": {
    "required_files": ["docs/HANDOFF_PHASE_{phase}.md"],
    "commands": [["{python}", "-m", "unittest", "discover", "-s", "tests"]],
    "invariants": ["no_credentials_in_source"],
    "claude_review_required": true,
    "debate_on_architecture_disagreement": true,
    "max_remediation_attempts": 4,
    "merge_policy": "auto",
    "allowed_paths": ["src/", "tests/", "pyproject.toml", "docs/HANDOFF_PHASE_{phase}.md"]
  },
  "phases": [
    {"number": 0, "name": "Foundation", "prompt": "prompts/phases/phase-00.md",
     "acceptance": {"merge_policy": "human"}},
    {"number": 1, "name": "First feature", "prompt": "prompts/phases/phase-01.md"}
  ]
}

Every key is described in Configuration. The implementer's --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox turns off Codex's own sandbox and approval prompts: buildctl already runs Codex inside its sandbox-exec profile, and an unattended run has no one to answer a prompt. See Trust and the sandbox for what that profile holds.

Phase prompts#

A phase prompt is a Markdown file that tells the implementer what to build. Good prompts name what already exists, what to add, which paths the phase may change, and what the handoff must record. The implementer also receives the phase's acceptance contract, so the prompt does not need to repeat the gate commands.

Prompts are governed files: an agent cannot change them, and a change you make takes effect only after you trust the new commit.

The acceptance contract#

phase_defaults is the contract every phase inherits. A phase overrides any part of it under acceptance, and {phase} in a path becomes the phase number.

  • Required files must exist after the implementer finishes.
  • Commands each run in the sandbox with no network and must exit 0. {python} resolves to an interpreter with the dependencies declared in the phase's pyproject.toml installed. Every dependency needs an upper bound (pkg>=1,<2), and only pre-built wheels are installed, so nothing from the agent's manifest executes as you. A command without {python} runs as written.
  • Allowed paths are the only paths the phase may change. Anything else, and any change to a governed file, fails the phase.
  • Invariants are named rules the reviewer checks the change against.

Prompts buildctl provides#

buildctl ships the output formats agents must return (PHASE_RESULT, REVIEW_RESULT, DEBATE_RESULT) and the default review and remediation prompts. They live in the package and are pinned with it. The formats cannot be overridden, because the code that validates them lives in buildctl too.

To tailor a prompt for one project, point roles.reviewer.review_prompt or roles.implementer.remediation_prompt at your own governed file. A review prompt must contain Protocol version: `buildctl-review-v2`.

4. Trust and the sandbox

buildctl refuses to run under rules or code you have not explicitly accepted.

What trust init pins#

buildctl trust init --to <sha> --confirm <sha> takes a full 40-character commit SHA, typed twice. It pins three things:

  • The governed files at that commit: build.yaml, AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, everything under prompts/ and templates/, and every file in governance_documents. buildctl reads them from its own read-only snapshot, never from your working tree, and fails the phase if an agent changes any of them.
  • The installed buildctl itself: its version and a digest of every file in the package.
  • The codex and claude executables, by path and hash.

buildctl trust show prints what is pinned.

When to trust again#

Run trust init again after you:

  • change any governed file. The change only takes effect once you trust the new commit.
  • upgrade, reinstall or edit buildctl. Until you do, buildctl refuses to start and shows both digests.
  • upgrade the codex or claude CLI. Until you do, the next call to it stops at AGENT_OPERATION_FAILED with <ROLE> _EXECUTABLE_INTEGRITY_FAILURE.

The console (buildctl-ui) is a separate package, so updating it never requires a new trust init.

Isolation conformance#

buildctl isolation verify probes the sandbox on this machine and records that it passed. It spends nothing.

Runs refuse to start once that record is over 24 hours old. The record is also bound to the sandbox policy and the trusted snapshot, so run isolation verify again after any trust init that changed governed files or followed a buildctl upgrade.

On macOS the sandbox is sandbox-exec. On Linux it is bubblewrap, and the record also pins its version and digest, so run isolation verify again after a bubblewrap upgrade too.

What the sandbox holds#

  • Agents work in a disposable clone with no remote.
  • Gate commands run with no network. Without network, nothing in the sandbox can reach a Unix socket on the host either, such as the Docker daemon or an SSH agent.
  • Agent output is checked before a single byte reaches your repository: only allowed, non-governed paths are copied, and the copy must match what the reviewer saw.
  • The canonical state, audit log and cost ledger live outside your repository, where agents cannot read them.

5. Running and watching

Starting work#

buildctl start runs every incomplete phase in order. buildctl run --until <N or milestone> stops after phase N or after a milestone named in build.yaml. buildctl phase <N> runs one phase, and refuses a phase that is already complete.

Only one buildctl process changes state at a time. A second one is refused while the first holds the state lock.

Watching a run#

buildctl status prints the state, the current phase, any pending approval or grant with its nonce, and today's spend. buildctl inspect prints everything a front end needs as one JSON document, and works before trust is set up. buildctl audit --after <seq> prints audit events after a sequence number.

The console shows the same information live: the phase line, the call in flight and its deadline, and spend by phase. See The console.

Pausing#

buildctl pause stops buildctl starting new work. A call already in flight finishes. buildctl resume allows new work again. Both take the state lock, so they cannot interrupt a run that is holding it.

The budget#

Each paid agent call has an estimated cost in operation_cost_usd. buildctl reserves that amount against max_daily_cost_usd before the call runs, and refuses the call if it would go over. The day is measured in UTC.

The ledger records estimates you configured, not your provider's bill.

Where state lives#

Canonical state, the hash-chained audit log, the cost ledger, the trusted snapshot and every agent artifact live outside your repository, in $XDG_STATE_HOME/buildctl/<hash of repo path> (by default ~/.local/state/buildctl/...). Set BUILDCTL_STATE_DIR to put it elsewhere.

FileWhat it holds
state.jsonThe build state: status, current phase, step, attempts, pending approval, operations.
audit.jsonlEvery state change, each event hash-chained to the one before.
costs.jsonlOne line per paid agent call reserved against the budget.
trust.json and snapshot/The trust anchor and the read-only copy of the governed files.
isolation-conformance.jsonThe last sandbox verification.
artifacts/phase-N/Agent results, review reports, gate results, debate requests and ADR proposals.

6. When it stops

buildctl stops with an escalation code whenever it cannot continue safely. buildctl status and the console's Stop view show the code and, where relevant, the nonce the fix needs. Each code below says what happened and what clears it.

The signal shapes match the console. A diamond is a wait buildctl planned for: nothing failed. A square is a stop: something failed, or a limit was hit and needs your grant. A dashed circle is an outcome nobody knows yet.

Waiting for you

  • CHECKPOINT_REQUIRED
  • DEBATE_REQUIRES_HUMAN

Stopped

  • REVIEW_BLOCKED
  • UNREVIEWABLE_DELTA
  • DEBATE_UNRESOLVED
  • STALE_DEBATE_RESULT
  • AUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED
  • DAILY_BUDGET_UNAVAILABLE
  • ADVANCE_PRECONDITIONS_UNMET
  • AGENT_OPERATION_FAILED
  • PHASE_DEADLINE_EXCEEDED
  • DELTA_CHANGED_AFTER_REVIEW
  • STALE_RUN
  • UNEXPECTED_FAILURE

Outcome unknown

  • UNKNOWN_EXTERNAL_OPERATION
  • OPERATION_TIMEOUT_UNKNOWN
  • STALE_RUN_UNKNOWN_OPERATION

Ceilings

  • PHASE_ATTEMPTS_EXHAUSTED
  • REMEDIATION_ATTEMPTS_EXHAUSTED
  • SEMANTIC_REVIEW_ATTEMPTS_EXHAUSTED
  • REVIEW_FORMAT_ATTEMPTS_EXHAUSTED
  • MAX_CONSECUTIVE_FAILURES_EXHAUSTED

Waiting for you#

CHECKPOINT_REQUIRED#

A phase in checkpoints.before_phases, a merge_policy: human merge, or the MVP milestone needs your approval.

Clear it: review the evidence, then approve. buildctl approve --nonce <n>, with the nonce from status. In the console, the Approve lever asks you to type the first 7 characters of the tree hash you reviewed. An approval made against state that has since moved is refused.

All stop codes

DEBATE_REQUIRES_HUMAN#

With roles.arbiter.mode: interactive, the review routed the phase to a debate, and the debate is yours to run. buildctl wrote DEBATE_REQUEST.json: the strategic findings, the evidence digest, the exact output format and the output_path to write the result to. The status detail is the request's path, in the phase's artifacts/phase-N/ directory.

Clear it: run the debate (for example with agent-debate), write the result to the request's output_path, then buildctl retry. A result that agrees becomes an ADR in decisions/ and is implemented. One that does not stops at DEBATE_UNRESOLVED.

This stop is a wait, not a failure: it does not count toward max_consecutive_failures. The debate call is still charged its configured operation_cost_usd.debate in the budget ledger. The Ledger lists the call as failed until the result is consumed.

All stop codes

Stopped#

REVIEW_BLOCKED#

The reviewer could not clear the phase.

Clear it: read the findings in artifacts/phase-N/REVIEW_RESULT-<n>.json in the state directory, or in the console's Stop view. Adjust the phase prompt or decide the question, then buildctl retry.

All stop codes

UNREVIEWABLE_DELTA#

The change has binary or oversized files the reviewer cannot read.

Clear it: adjust the phase so its output is reviewable, then buildctl retry.

All stop codes

DEBATE_UNRESOLVED#

The debate ended without agreement.

Clear it: decide the question, adjust the phase prompt, then buildctl retry.

All stop codes

STALE_DEBATE_RESULT#

The debate result was written for a different phase or base commit.

Clear it: run the debate again for the current request, then buildctl retry.

All stop codes

AUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED#

An agent CLI is logged out.

Clear it: log in (codex login or claude auth login), then buildctl retry.

All stop codes

DAILY_BUDGET_UNAVAILABLE#

The next agent call would exceed max_daily_cost_usd.

Clear it: wait for tomorrow (UTC), or raise the limit and trust the new commit, then buildctl retry.

All stop codes

ADVANCE_PRECONDITIONS_UNMET#

The phase passed review, but the budget ledger or a required approval no longer checks out.

Clear it: fix what the detail names, then buildctl retry.

All stop codes

AGENT_OPERATION_FAILED#

An agent call failed. The status detail starts with a detail code, then a redacted reason. Find the code below. <ROLE> is IMPLEMENTER, REVIEWER or ARBITER. <KIND> is the role, or DEBATE for an interactive debate result.

Clear it: do what the detail code's row says, then buildctl retry.

Detail codeWhat happenedClear it
<ROLE> _EXECUTABLE_UNAVAILABLE#The agent CLI is not where trust pinned it, or not on PATH.Reinstall it, run trust init again, then retry.
<ROLE> _EXECUTABLE_INTEGRITY_FAILURE#The agent CLI changed since trust init, usually an upgrade.Run trust init again to pin the new binary, then retry.
<ROLE> _AUTH_MODE_INVALID#roles.<role>.auth_mode is not environment, host_cli or none.Fix build.yaml, commit, trust the commit, then retry.
<ROLE> _PROCESS_FAILED#The agent CLI exited with an error. Its own message follows the colon.Read that message: a rate limit, an expired login or a model error. Fix it, then retry.
<ROLE>_SECRET_OUTPUT#A credential appeared in the agent's output or result file, so nothing was stored. The detail names the source and the credential kind, never the value.Rotate that credential. Find why the agent printed it, then retry.
REVIEWER_MUTATED_WORKSPACE#The reviewer changed files during a read-only review.Check the reviewer command still limits it to --tools Read,Grep,Glob, then retry.
IMPLEMENTER_OUTPUT_SCHEMA_INVALID#The implementer's PHASE_RESULT did not have the contract's fields.Retry. If it repeats, check the phase prompt does not ask for another format.
<KIND> _OUTPUT_MISSING#The agent finished without writing a result.Retry. If it repeats, check the agent command writes to {output} or prints its result.
<KIND>_OUTPUT_EMPTY#The result file was empty.Retry.
<KIND> _OUTPUT_INVALID_JSON#The result was not valid JSON. The detail quotes the text near the error.Retry. If it repeats, check the phase prompt does not ask for prose around the JSON.
<KIND> _OUTPUT_NOT_OBJECT#The result was JSON, but not an object.Retry.

A reviewer's malformed report never stops here: it is retried, and counts toward REVIEW_FORMAT_ATTEMPTS_EXHAUSTED.

All stop codes

PHASE_DEADLINE_EXCEEDED#

The phase ran past max_phase_minutes.

Clear it: buildctl retry. A retry starts a new attempt with a fresh deadline.

All stop codes

DELTA_CHANGED_AFTER_REVIEW#

What would be committed differs from what the reviewer attested. This should never happen. Nothing was committed.

Clear it: investigate before retrying, because a retry starts a fresh attempt and the evidence moves on. In the state directory, the last review_reduced event in audit.jsonl holds the delta_id the reviewer saw, and workspace in state.json is the phase workspace that holds what would have been committed. Something changed one of them after review: a process writing into the workspace, or a different allowed_paths. Once you know which, buildctl retry.

All stop codes

STALE_RUN#

The last run died between agent calls.

Clear it: buildctl retry.

All stop codes

UNEXPECTED_FAILURE#

The supervisor hit an error it does not classify.

Clear it: read the detail, fix the cause, then buildctl retry.

All stop codes

Outcome unknown#

An agent call may or may not have finished. buildctl never guesses: you settle each unknown call before anything else runs.

UNKNOWN_EXTERNAL_OPERATION#

An agent call was started and its outcome was never recorded.

Clear it: buildctl reconcile --operation <id> --action accept-output to keep the output it left, or --action authorize-retry to discard it and pay for a new call.

All stop codes

OPERATION_TIMEOUT_UNKNOWN#

An agent call timed out, so its outcome is unknown.

Clear it: buildctl reconcile --operation <id> --action accept-output to keep the output it left, or --action authorize-retry to discard it and pay for a new call.

All stop codes

STALE_RUN_UNKNOWN_OPERATION#

The last run died with agent calls in flight.

Clear it: reconcile each unknown call with buildctl reconcile --operation <id> --action <accept-output or authorize-retry>, then buildctl retry.

All stop codes

Ceilings#

A ceiling stops the build when a limit is hit. buildctl retry --authorize-extra-attempt --nonce <n> buys exactly one more pass past that ceiling, for that phase only, and the grant is spent on use. Or fix the cause first.

PHASE_ATTEMPTS_EXHAUSTED#

A new attempt would exceed max_phase_attempts.

Clear it: buildctl retry --authorize-extra-attempt --nonce <n>, with the nonce from status, buys one more attempt. Or fix the cause first.

All stop codes

REMEDIATION_ATTEMPTS_EXHAUSTED#

Another remediation lap would exceed the phase's max_remediation_attempts.

Clear it: buildctl retry --authorize-extra-attempt --nonce <n>, with the nonce from status, buys one more lap. Or fix the cause first.

All stop codes

SEMANTIC_REVIEW_ATTEMPTS_EXHAUSTED#

Another review would exceed max_semantic_review_attempts.

Clear it: buildctl retry --authorize-extra-attempt --nonce <n>, with the nonce from status, buys one more review. Or fix the cause first.

All stop codes

REVIEW_FORMAT_ATTEMPTS_EXHAUSTED#

The reviewer's report was rejected as malformed max_review_format_attempts times. Each rejection's reason is in the audit log as review_format_rejected.

Clear it: read the reasons, fix the review prompt if it caused them, then buildctl retry --authorize-extra-attempt --nonce <n>, with the nonce from status.

All stop codes

MAX_CONSECUTIVE_FAILURES_EXHAUSTED#

The build stopped max_consecutive_failures times in a row.

Clear it: fix what keeps failing, then buildctl retry --authorize-extra-attempt --nonce <n>, with the nonce from status. Authorizing it also resets the streak.

All stop codes

7. The console

buildctl-ui is an optional companion: a local web console and a terminal UI over the same build. It lives in ui/ as its own package, so editing it never changes what trust init pins.

buildctl-ui          # the web console, for the repository you are in
buildctl-ui tui      # the same in the terminal

What it shows#

ViewWhat it is for
LineThe phase line, the call in flight, spend by phase, and the levers you can pull now.
StopWhy the build stopped, the evidence (findings, agent calls, gates, artifacts), and only the levers the kernel will accept.
PhasesEvery phase with its attempts, reviews, fixes, debates and cost.
LedgerThe audit chain, newest first, filterable by phase and event.
SetupReadiness in the order buildctl checks it, and the trust levers.

Keys 1 to 5 switch views in both surfaces.

Levers and their conditions#

Every action is a numbered lever listing the conditions that allow or lock it. The numbers are fixed: Start is 01, Approve is 04, Retry is 05, and so on, in both surfaces. The conditions come from the kernel, so the console never offers an action buildctl would refuse.

Typing the evidence#

Approving, pinning trust, buying an extra attempt and reconciling ask you to type the evidence you looked at: the tree-hash prefix for an approval, the commit for trust, the phase number for a grant, the operation for a reconcile. The console sends the nonce it showed you, so an approval made against state that has since moved is refused. A signed action leaves a receipt on screen.

Runs outlive the console#

Start runs detached. Closing the console never stops a build.

Security#

The web console listens on 127.0.0.1 only. Every request needs the token in the link buildctl-ui prints, reads included, because the state holds pending nonces. The Host header must name the console, and state changes must be JSON from the console's own origin.

8. Reference

Commands#

Global flags: --repo <path> (must be the repository toplevel) and --dry-run.

CommandWhat it does
start#Run every incomplete phase in order.
run --until <N or milestone>#Run up to phase N, or a milestone named in build.yaml.
phase <N>#Run one phase. Refused if it is already complete.
status#State, current phase, any pending approval or grant (with its nonce), and today's spend.
pause#Stop starting new work.
resume#Allow it again.
approve --nonce <n>#Approve the pending checkpoint. The nonce comes from status.
retry#Try again after an ordinary failure. Starts a fresh attempt. --authorize-extra-attempt --nonce <n> buys exactly one more pass past an exhausted ceiling.
reconcile --operation <id> --action <action>#Settle an agent call whose outcome is unknown. The action is accept-output (keep what it left) or authorize-retry (discard it and pay for a new call).
trust init --to <sha> --confirm <sha>#Pin the governed files at that commit, this buildctl, and both agent executables.
trust show#Show what is pinned.
isolation verify#Probe the sandbox and record that it passed. Runs refuse to start once that record is over 24 hours old.
auth check#Confirm both agent CLIs are logged in.
bootstrap#Create the build state. Requires fresh isolation conformance.
validate#Check build.yaml.
inspect#The full read model as one JSON document: state, phases, trust, isolation, budget, the stop and its meaning, and every action with the conditions that allow or lock it. Read-only.
audit --after <seq>#Audit events after a sequence number, as JSON. --limit caps how many.

Configuration#

KeyMeaning
limits.max_phase_attempts#Attempts a phase may start before PHASE_ATTEMPTS_EXHAUSTED.

9. Guarantees and limits

What buildctl guarantees#

  • Agents never touch your repository, state or budget. They work in a disposable clone with no remote, and buildctl alone copies their output in.
  • Only reviewed bytes are committed. What is committed must match what the reviewer saw, or the phase stops with DELTA_CHANGED_AFTER_REVIEW.
  • Governed files stay governed. No phase can change build.yaml, prompts, templates or governance documents.
  • Nothing runs under rules you did not trust. buildctl reads governed files from its trusted snapshot, so a change in your working tree has no effect until you trust the new commit. A changed buildctl or agent executable stops buildctl until you do.
  • No call spends past the budget. Each call is reserved against the daily limit before it runs.
  • A crash is accounted for. Every step is recorded before and after it runs. An agent call whose outcome is unknown stays unknown until you reconcile it.
  • Every state change is recorded. The audit log is hash-chained, so editing or removing an event breaks the chain and buildctl refuses to load the state.

What it does not guarantee#

  • That the code is correct. The review is adversarial, not a proof. Your acceptance commands are the only executable check.
  • A compliance-grade ledger. The audit chain is tamper-evident, not signed or externally anchored.
  • Your real cost. The budget counts the estimates in operation_cost_usd, not your provider's bill.

Current limitations#

  • On Linux, the host must allow unprivileged user namespaces. Stock containers do not, so buildctl refuses to run in them. See Running on Linux.
  • On Linux, a role with network access reaches the whole network. There is no per-host allowlist yet.
  • The implementer is assumed to be Codex and the reviewer Claude. auth check, credential staging and parts of config validation are written for those two CLIs.
  • Dependency provisioning for acceptance commands is Python-only (pyproject.toml, {python}).
  • With arbiter.mode set to anything but interactive, the arbiter command only receives {prompt} and {output}. A command that uses {phase}, {review} or {rounds} fails. Use interactive debates.
